danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 24
paragraphs: Den klare aften den femogtyvende august lå fyrst Andrej støttet på albuen i et faldefærdigt skur i landsbyen Knjazkovo i den fjerneste ende af sit regiments lejrplads. Gennem et hul i den revnede væg kunne han se, bag træhegnet, en række tredive år gamle birketræer med de nedre grene hugget af, en mark med havreneg og nogle buske, bag hvilke røgen fra lejrbål steg op — soldaternes køkkener.
Snævert, tyngende og nytteløst for enhver, som hans liv nu syntes ham, følte fyrst Andrej sig aftenen før et slag lige så ophidset og irritabel, som han havde gjort syv år tidligere ved Austerlitz.

Han havde modtaget og givet ordrerne til næste dags slag og havde intet mere at gøre. Men hans tanker — de enkleste, klareste og derfor mest forfærdende — lod ham ikke i fred. Han vidste, at morgendagens slag ville blive det mest frygtelige af alle, han havde deltaget i, og for første gang i sit liv trængte muligheden for at dø sig ind på ham — ikke i forhold til noget verdsligt og heller ikke med henblik på virkningen for andre, men simpelthen i forhold til ham selv, hans egen sjæl — levende, klart, forfærdeligt og næsten som en vished. Og fra dette perspektiv blev alt, hvad der før havde pint og optaget ham, pludselig belyst af et koldt, hvidt lys uden skygger, uden perspektiv, uden konturer. Hele livet syntes ham som lanternebilleder, han længe havde betragtet ved kunstigt lys gennem et glas. Nu så han pludselig disse dårligt malede billeder i dagslys og uden glasset. »Ja, ja! Der er de, de falske billeder, der ophidsede, henrev og pinte mig,« sagde han til sig selv, mens han gennemgik livets lanternebilleders vigtigste motiver og nu betragtede dem i det kolde, hvide lys fra sin klare bevidsthed om døden. »Der er de, de groft malede figurer, der engang syntes storslåede og mystiske. Ære, samfundets vel, kærlighed til en kvinde, selve fædrelandet — hvor vigtige disse billeder syntes mig, med hvilken dyb mening de syntes at være fyldt! Og alt er så enkelt, blegt og groft i det kolde, hvide lys fra denne morgen, jeg føler er ved at bryde frem for mig.« De tre store sorger i hans liv optog ham særligt: hans kærlighed til en kvinde, hans fars død og den franske invasion, der havde oversvømmet det halve Rusland. »Kærlighed... den lille pige, der syntes mig at svælge over af mystiske kræfter! Ja, sandelig, jeg elskede hende. Jeg lagde romantiske planer om kærlighed og lykke med hende! Åh, sikken en dreng jeg var!« sagde han højt og bittert. »Min Gud! Jeg troede på en ideel kærlighed, der ville holde hende tro mod mig i hele det år, jeg var borte! Som den blide due i fabelen skulle hun vansmægte adskilt fra mig.... Men det var langt enklere i virkeligheden.... Det hele var meget enkelt og forfærdeligt.«

»Da min far byggede Lyse Bakker, troede han, at stedet var hans: hans jord, hans luft, hans bønder. Men Napoleon kom og fejede ham til side, uvidende om hans eksistens, som han kunne børste en spån fra sin vej, og hans Lyse Bakker og hele hans liv faldt fra hinanden. Fyrstinde Marja siger, det er en prøvelse sendt fra oven. Men hvad for en prøvelse, når han ikke er her og aldrig vender tilbage? Han er her ikke! Hvem gælder prøvelsen så? Fædrelandet, Moskvas ødelæggelse! Og i morgen bliver jeg dræbt, måske ikke engang af en franskmand, men af en af vore egne, af en soldat, der affyrer sin musket tæt ved mit øre, som en af dem gjorde i går, og franskmændene vil komme og tage mig i hoved og fødder og slænge mig i et hul, for at jeg ikke skal stinke dem i næsen, og nye livsvilkår vil opstå, som vil synes ganske almindelige for andre, og som jeg intet skal vide om. Jeg vil ikke eksistere mere....«

Han så på birkerækken, der skinnede i solskinnet med sine ubevægelige grønne og gule blade og hvide bark. »At dø... at blive dræbt i morgen... At jeg ikke skulle eksistere... At alt dette stadig ville være til, men uden mig....«

Og birketræerne med deres lys og skygge, de krøllede skyer, røgen fra lejrbålene og alt omkring ham forandrede sig og syntes forfærdeligt og truende. En kulde løb ned ad hans ryg. Han rejste sig hurtigt, gik ud af skuret og begyndte at vandre omkring.
Da han var vendt tilbage, hørtes stemmer udenfor skuret. »Hvem er det?« råbte han.

Den rødnæsede kaptajn Timokhin, tidligere Dolokhov (den degraderede officers) eskadronschef, men nu af mangel på officerer blevet bataljonschef, trådte forsigtigt ind i skuret, fulgt af en adjutant og regimentets kasserer.
Fyrst Andrej rejste sig hastigt, lyttede til de sager, de kom med, gav nogle yderligere instrukser og var ved at sende dem bort, da han hørte en velkendt, lispende stemme bag skuret.
»Pokkers også!« sagde stemmen af en mand, der snublede over noget.

Fyrst Andrej kiggede ud af skuret og så Pierre, der var snublet over en pæl og næsten faldet, komme hen imod ham. Det var fyrst Andrej ubehageligt at møde folk fra sin egen kreds i almindelighed, og Pierre i særdeleshed, for han mindede ham om alle de smertelige øjeblikke ved hans sidste besøg i Moskva.
»Dig? Sikken en overraskelse!« sagde han. »Hvad bringer dig hid? Det havde jeg ikke ventet!«

Idet han sagde dette, udtrykte hans øjne og ansigt mere end kulde — de udtrykte fjendtlighed, som Pierre straks lagde mærke til. Han var kommet hen til skuret fuld af iver, men da han så fyrst Andrejs ansigt, følte han sig beklemt og ilde til mode.
»Jeg er kommet... bare... du véd... kommet... det interesserer mig,« sagde Pierre, der så ofte den dag meningsløst havde gentaget ordet »interesserer«. »Jeg vil gerne se slaget.«
»Nå ja, og hvad siger frimurerne om krig? Hvordan vil de standse den?« sagde fyrst Andrej sarkastisk. »Nå, og hvad med Moskva? Og mine folk? Er de nået til Moskva til sidst?« spurgte han alvorligt.
»Ja, det er de. Julie Drubetskaja fortalte mig det. Jeg opsøgte dem, men gik glip af dem. De er rejst til jeres gods nær Moskva.«

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: On that bright evening of August 25, Prince Andrew lay propped on his elbow in a broken-down shed in the village of Knyazkovo at the far end of his regiment's camp. Through a gap in the broken wall he could see, beside the wooden fence, a row of thirty-year-old birches with their lower branches trimmed off, a field with sheaves of oats standing in it, and some bushes near which rose the smoke of campfires—the soldiers' kitchens.
Narrow and burdensome and useless to anyone as his life now seemed to him, Prince Andrew on the eve of battle felt as agitated and irritable as he had seven years before at Austerlitz.

He had received and given the orders for the next day's battle and had nothing more to do. But his thoughts—the simplest, clearest, and therefore most terrible thoughts—would give him no peace. He knew that tomorrow's battle would be the most terrible he had ever been in, and for the first time in his life, the possibility of death presented itself not in relation to any worldly matter or its effect on others, but simply in relation to himself, to his own soul—vividly, plainly, terribly, and almost as a certainty. And from the height of this awareness, all that had previously tormented and preoccupied him was suddenly illuminated by a cold white light without shadows, without perspective, without distinction. All of life appeared to him like magic-lantern pictures he had long been gazing at through a glass by artificial light. Now he suddenly saw those badly painted images in the clear daylight, without the glass. "Yes, yes! There they are, those false images that excited, enchanted, and tormented me," he said to himself, reviewing the principal pictures of the magic lantern of life and seeing them now in the cold white light of his clear perception of death. "There they are, those crudely painted figures that once seemed splendid and mysterious. Glory, the good of society, love of a woman, the Fatherland itself—how important these pictures seemed, with what profound meaning they appeared to be filled! And it is all so simple, pale, and crude in the cold white light of this morning I feel dawning for me." The three great sorrows of his life held his attention in particular: his love for a woman, his father's death, and the French invasion that had overrun half of Russia. "Love... that little girl who seemed to me overflowing with mysterious power! Yes, I loved her. I made romantic plans of love and happiness with her! Oh, what a fool I was!" he said aloud bitterly. "I believed in some ideal love that was to keep her faithful for the whole year of my absence! Like the gentle dove in the fable, she was to pine apart from me... But it was much simpler than that... It was all very simple and horrible."

"When my father built Bald Hills, he thought the place was his: his land, his air, his peasants. But Napoleon came and swept him aside, unconscious of his existence, as he might brush a chip from his path, and his Bald Hills and his whole life fell to pieces. Princess Mary says it is a trial sent from above. What is the trial for, when he is gone and will never return? He is gone! For whom then is the trial intended? The Fatherland, the destruction of Moscow! And tomorrow I shall be killed—perhaps not even by a Frenchman but by one of our own men, by a soldier firing a musket close to my ear, as one of them did yesterday—and the French will come and take me by the head and feet and fling me into a ditch so I won't stink under their noses, and new conditions of life will arise that will seem perfectly ordinary to others but about which I shall know nothing. I shall not exist..."

He looked at the row of birches shining in the sunshine, with their motionless green and yellow foliage and white bark. "To die... to be killed tomorrow... That I should not exist... That all this should still be, but not me..."

And the birches with their light and shade, the curly clouds, the smoke of the campfires, and everything around him changed and seemed terrible and menacing. A cold shiver ran down his spine. He rose quickly, went out of the shed, and began pacing.
When he returned, voices were heard outside the shed. "Who's that?" he called.

The red-nosed Captain Timokhin, formerly Dolokhov's company commander but now, due to the shortage of officers, a battalion commander, shyly entered the shed followed by an adjutant and the regimental paymaster.
Prince Andrew rose quickly, listened to the business they had come about, gave them additional instructions, and was about to dismiss them when he heard a familiar, lisping voice behind the shed.
"Devil take it!" said the voice of a man stumbling over something.

Prince Andrew looked out of the shed and saw Pierre, who had tripped over a pole on the ground and nearly fallen, coming his way. It was unpleasant to Prince Andrew to meet people from his own circle in general, and Pierre especially, for Pierre reminded him of all the painful moments of his last visit to Moscow.
"You? What a surprise!" he said. "What brings you here? This is unexpected!"

As he said this, his eyes and face expressed more than coldness—they expressed hostility, which Pierre noticed at once. He had approached the shed full of animation, but seeing Prince Andrew's face, he felt constrained and uncomfortable.
"I've come... simply... you know... come... it interests me," said Pierre, who had so often that day senselessly repeated the word "interesting." "I wanted to see the battle."

"Oh yes, and what do the Masonic brothers say about war? How would they stop it?" said Prince Andrew sarcastically. "Well, and how's Moscow? And my family? Have they reached Moscow at last?" he asked more seriously.
"Yes, they have. Julie Drubetskaya told me. I went to see them but missed them. They've gone to your estate near Moscow."
